subject: Habitat Goods + Overhaul: a full-funnel audit (unsolicited, but worth 5 minutes)
snippet: Hi Jordan, I know cold agency pitches are the last thing your inbox needs, so I'll try to make this one worth the five minutes. We're Overhaul Digital — a 40-person performance mar
body_text:
Hi Jordan,

I know cold agency pitches are the last thing your inbox needs, so I'll try to make this one worth the five minutes.

We're Overhaul Digital — a 40-person performance marketing agency that works exclusively with DTC brands in the $20M-$100M revenue range, mostly home, outdoor, and lifestyle categories. Before reaching out, we ran a light external audit of Habitat Goods' public-facing paid social presence (ad library, landing pages, and your Klaviyo sign-up flow, since that's visible without account access). A few things stood out:

1. Your top-performing static ad (the walnut console table, running since roughly early June based on library timestamps) has been live for 6+ weeks without a creative refresh. Our data across similar accounts shows CPMs typically start climbing on a single creative around week 5 as audience fatigue sets in — worth checking your frequency metric if you haven't already.

2. Your homepage-to-signup flow asks for email before showing any incentive copy above the fold. In split tests we've run for comparable brands, leading with the offer (e.g., '15% off your first order') before the form field lifted signup conversion by 18-24%.

3. Your SMS opt-in isn't currently offered as a secondary CTA anywhere in the checkout flow we could find — most brands your size are running SMS at 20-30% of email list size at this point, and it's typically an incremental win rather than cannibalizing email.

None of this is meant as a knock — a lot of it is genuinely solid, and the brand voice across your ad creative is more consistent than most accounts we audit unprompted.

We'd love the chance to put together a fuller audit (free, no obligation) if it's ever useful timing-wise, particularly if you're evaluating your agency mix heading into next year's planning. Case studies from two comparable home goods accounts are available on request — happy to share names privately rather than in a cold email.

One last note, since I know unsolicited audits can read as a pretext for a pitch: we're not looking to replace your existing agency-of-record relationship wholesale, and we'd say so directly if that's not a fit. Most of our current home-goods clients came to us for a specific, bounded engagement — usually a paid social creative sprint or a checkout conversion project — and a few expanded from there once trust was established, but several stayed exactly at that scope, which is fine by us.

If now's not the moment, no worries at all — feel free to keep this for later or ignore entirely.

Best,
Renata Silva
Partner, Overhaul Digital
renata@overhauldigital.com | overhauldigital.com | (646) 555-0113

subject: Agency renewal - where I've landed before Thursday's call
snippet: Sofia, Wanted to get ahead of this before it lands on your desk as a surprise line item in the FY27 budget review. Fold & Field sent over their renewal terms for the SOW that expir
body_text:
Sofia,

Wanted to get ahead of this before it lands on your desk as a surprise line item in the FY27 budget review. Fold & Field sent over their renewal terms for the SOW that expires September 1, and I want to walk you through where I've landed and why, since it's a meaningful increase.

THE ASK: They're proposing the monthly retainer move from $22,000 to $25,500, with the increase justified by formalizing TikTok content production as a scoped deliverable rather than the ad hoc billing we've been doing all year. Separately from that, they haven't taken a rate increase in the two years we've worked with them, which given agency comp inflation is honestly reasonable on its face.

WHAT I'VE VALIDATED: I pulled our actual TikTok spend with them for the trailing 12 months - we paid roughly $2,800/month in ad hoc production fees on top of the base retainer, so the "new" $3,500/month increase is only about $700/month more than what we're already spending unofficially. Framed that way, this isn't really a $42K/year new cost, it's closer to $8,400/year in true incremental spend, with the benefit of predictable invoicing and a formal SLA around TikTok turnaround times, which has been a pain point - Cam's flagged more than once that ad hoc TikTok requests get deprioritized against retainer-covered work.

WHERE I HAVE CONCERNS: Their creative production line (shoot days, editing) hasn't changed in scope but the base retainer for that work is going up too as part of the "modest rate adjustment," and I don't have great visibility into whether that portion is fair market or just came along for the ride with the TikTok ask. I've asked Tessa for a scope-by-scope breakdown rather than one bundled number so we can evaluate each piece on its own, and I'll push on that Thursday.

MY RECOMMENDATION: I think we renew, with TikTok formalized, but I want to negotiate the base retainer increase down or get something added in exchange - options include an extra shoot day per quarter, or holding the base rate flat and only paying for TikTok as new incremental scope. I also want a 60-day-or-less termination clause preserved given how much of our Q4 execution now runs through them.

I don't need a decision from you today, but I do want your gut check before I go into Thursday's call, and I'll loop Wes in parallel on whether $25,500-30,000/mo range is even fundable given everything else in the FY27 marketing budget. Let me know if you want 15 minutes before Thursday or if written is fine.

Jordan

Jordan Feld
VP Marketing, Habitat Goods

subject: The State of Marketing 2026: what 1,400 marketers told us
snippet: We surveyed 1,400 marketing leaders across DTC, B2B, and services businesses for our annual State of Marketing report. A few findings worth your time this planning season. Budget a
body_text:
We surveyed 1,400 marketing leaders across DTC, B2B, and services businesses for our annual State of Marketing report. A few findings worth your time this planning season.

Budget allocation is shifting again. Paid social remains the largest single line item for consumer brands (averaging 34% of paid budget), but the growth is now coming from retail media and creator partnerships rather than traditional programmatic display, which fell for the third straight year. Teams that reallocated more than 15% of budget toward retail media in the last 12 months reported blended CAC improvements averaging 9%, though the range was wide and heavily dependent on category.

AI adoption has moved past the experimentation phase for most respondents. 68% now use generative tools for first-draft copy, and 41% use them for creative testing at scale — but only 22% have a formal review process to catch brand-voice drift, which correlates with a rise in customer complaints about 'off' tone in automated messaging. If your team is leaning on AI drafts for lifecycle or paid social copy, this is worth a look before your Q4 volume ramps.

Attribution remains the top frustration. 54% of respondents rated their current attribution model as 'somewhat' or 'not at all' reliable, and multi-touch models are losing ground to simpler incrementality testing as privacy changes continue to erode platform-reported data. Brands running quarterly holdout tests report significantly higher confidence in reallocating budget mid-quarter than those relying solely on platform attribution.

Team structure is consolidating. The average headcount-per-function ratio for a 150-250 person DTC company now favors generalist 'growth marketer' roles over narrow channel specialists, a reversal from three years ago. Respondents cited faster iteration and lower coordination overhead as the driver, though several noted a steeper ramp time for new hires without deep channel expertise.

Retention investment is up sharply. 61% of respondents increased lifecycle/retention budget year over year, the largest shift of any category we tracked, as acquisition costs continue to climb across paid channels.

The full 64-page report, including channel-by-channel benchmarks and a downloadable budget planning template, is available now. We built the benchmarks to be filterable by company size and vertical, so home goods and DTC-specific cuts are available if you download the interactive version rather than the static PDF.

A few smaller findings that didn't make the headline list but are worth a skim if you're building next year's plan: brands running quarterly creative refresh cycles reported meaningfully lower CPMs than brands refreshing twice a year, though the sample size on this cut was smaller than we'd like. Marketing teams that shared a single source-of-truth dashboard with finance reported faster budget reallocation decisions mid-quarter than teams reconciling numbers across separate tools. And headcount growth in marketing organizations broadly lagged revenue growth for the second year running, which respondents attributed partly to AI-assisted productivity gains and partly to simple budget caution given the macro environment.

We also asked respondents to rank their top three unsolved problems heading into next year. Attribution reliability topped the list, followed closely by creative production velocity — keeping pace with the volume of assets needed across paid social, lifecycle, and organic without ballooning the creative team. Third was cross-functional alignment with finance on how to model marketing's contribution to revenue, an old problem that apparently hasn't gotten any easier despite years of better tooling.

If you only have ten minutes, skip to the executive summary and the budget allocation chapter — those two sections cover most of what tends to matter for Q4 planning conversations with leadership.

snippet: Hi Jordan, Monthly status update for the replatform migration ahead of our sync on Monday. Here's where things stand as of this morning. COMPLETED SINCE LAST UPDATE: - Product cata
body_text:
Hi Jordan,

Monthly status update for the replatform migration ahead of our sync on Monday. Here's where things stand as of this morning.

COMPLETED SINCE LAST UPDATE:
- Product catalog import: all 1,140 SKUs migrated from the legacy Magento instance into Shopify Plus, including variant options and metafields for the collection taxonomy your team built.
- Redirect map: 480 legacy URLs mapped to their Shopify equivalents to protect SEO equity, submitted to Denise's team for a spot check.
- Theme build: PDP, PLP, and homepage templates are functional on staging, built against the current brand system.

IN PROGRESS:
- Inventory sync between the new platform and your 3PL (Deliverr) is the long pole right now. We found a mismatch in how bundle SKUs report available quantity that's taking longer to resolve than scoped - roughly a week behind where I hoped we'd be.
- Klaviyo integration for email/SMS is connected and passing test events, but historical customer profile data (purchase history specifically) is still backfilling, expected done by end of month.
- Payment processing: Shopify Payments is live in test mode, Braintree fallback still needs configuration for the small percentage of international orders you flagged as a requirement.

RISKS TO FLAG:
- The inventory sync delay puts real pressure on our target cutover date. If it slips another two weeks we're cutting it close to your holiday campaign launch, and I don't want to be the reason Gather launches on a broken cart experience.
- We have not yet load-tested checkout under Black-Friday-level concurrent traffic. I'd like to schedule that for the first week of September at the latest, which means we need a stable checkout build about two weeks before that.

PROPOSED REVISED TIMELINE:
- Aug 1: inventory sync resolved, bundle SKU issue closed
- Aug 15: full site freeze for QA on staging
- Sept 1: load test
- Sept 15: cutover, roughly two weeks later than the original plan

I know that's not the news you wanted given Gather launches in early November, but it still gives comfortable runway before peak. Let's align on Monday and I can walk through the bundle SKU issue in more detail if useful.

A couple of other items for the sync: QA coverage right now spans Chrome, Safari, and Edge on desktop plus Safari and Chrome on mobile, which covers about 94% of your current traffic mix per the analytics export you sent in April. I don't think we need broader coverage than that, but flag if your assumptions have changed. On SEO, beyond the redirect map, we've also rebuilt the structured data (product schema, breadcrumbs) since the legacy site's markup was out of date and was probably costing you some rich-result real estate in search already.

Last thing - once inventory sync is resolved, I'd like to run a full content audit against the legacy site to make sure nothing customer-facing got dropped in the migration, things like the sizing guide PDFs and the FAQ accordion content tend to get missed. I can have someone on my team start that in parallel with the sync fix so it doesn't add time to the critical path.

Kyle

Hi Jordan,

Monthly replatform status: catalog migration and redirect map are done; inventory sync with Deliverr is the long pole and we're about a week behind. Proposed revised cutover: Sept 15.

Let's align Monday.

Kyle

Team — Q4 is our biggest revenue quarter and I want us aligned going in rather than scrambling in October, so here's how I want to organize the next eight weeks. Read the whole thing, there's a section relevant to each of you.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Last year we hit our BFCM number but burned out doing it — creative was still being approved the week of launch, the lifecycle flows went out with typos because we were rushing, and Wes was chasing final actuals into January. I'd like this year to feel different, not because we're being less ambitious but because we're starting earlier and locking decisions sooner.

TIMELINE
- Now through July 25: creative concepting and shot list finalization. Photoshoot is Aug 4-5.
- July 25 - Aug 22: build phase — lifecycle flows, landing pages, paid social creative variants, all built off approved assets, no new concepting after this point unless something is actively broken.
- Aug 22 - Sept 5: QA and dry runs. Every flow gets a real send test, every landing page gets a real device/browser pass.
- Sept 5 onward: live, iterate based on data, no more structural changes, just optimization.

OWNERSHIP
- Cam: all copy, lookbook draft due July 24
- Rachel: all visual assets, shot list due July 25, homepage comps due Aug 15
- Ben: lifecycle flows, BFCM sequence build starting July 28
- Nina: paid social creative testing plan and the retention experiment we discussed, results before flows lock
- Wes: budget tracking, I want a weekly actuals-vs-plan number starting in August, not a surprise in January
- Denise: replatform coordination, I know that timeline is still shaky and I'm tracking it separately with you and Sofia

BUDGET
Total Q4 marketing spend is $120K paid social, $34K paid search, $28K influencer/partnerships, and the existing agency retainer. I'll send the full deck separately this week — Sofia's seen the top-line already.

One ask: if you're blocked on anything, tell me immediately, not at the weekly sync. A three-day delay in July becomes a missed BFCM deadline in October. I'd rather over-communicate than have anyone quietly behind.

RISKS I'M WATCHING
- The replatform timeline is the thing most likely to blow up this plan. If Sept 1 slips past Sept 15, we're rebuilding half of this calendar on the fly, so Denise and I are tracking that separately and I'll flag early if it's trending the wrong way.
- Agency capacity during the SOW renewal conversation — I don't want contract negotiations to slow down deliverables, so Tessa's team has been told the renewal talk is separate from the Q4 production timeline and shouldn't affect it either way.
- Creative approval bottlenecks, historically the thing that eats our buffer. I'm committing to 48-hour turnaround on anything routed to me for sign-off this quarter, and I'd ask the same of everyone else in the chain.

Excited for this one. Let's go build something we're proud of.

subject: Adweek Daily: retail media's next fight, agency layoffs, and a very online rebrand
snippet: Good morning. Here's what the industry is talking about today. RETAIL MEDIA'S NEXT FIGHT: Three of the largest retail media networks are quietly renegotiating minimum spend commitm
body_text:
Good morning. Here's what the industry is talking about today.

RETAIL MEDIA'S NEXT FIGHT: Three of the largest retail media networks are quietly renegotiating minimum spend commitments with mid-market brands, according to five media buyers we spoke with. The networks say it's about data quality tiers; buyers say it's a floor increase in disguise. Either way, if you're under $500K annual spend on any single network, expect a call from your rep this quarter.

AGENCY LAYOFFS: A mid-size independent shop in Chicago cut 8% of staff this week, mostly in paid media, citing client consolidation onto in-house teams. It's the third such cut we've tracked this month among agencies serving consumer brands under $50M revenue — a segment that's increasingly bringing performance marketing in-house while keeping creative and brand work with outside partners.

A VERY ONLINE REBRAND: A DTC mattress brand's overnight logo change sparked over 40,000 posts calling it a downgrade. The brand hasn't responded publicly, but internal sources say the switch was tied to a packaging cost reduction, not purely aesthetic choice — a reminder that 'why' rarely survives contact with the internet.

NUMBER OF THE DAY: 61%. The share of marketers in a new industry survey who say they increased lifecycle/retention budget this year, even as overall marketing budgets held flat or shrank. Acquisition costs are the stated driver across nearly every category we cover.

WORTH YOUR TIME: A long read on how three home goods brands are handling the shift away from third-party cookies in their paid social measurement — worth a skim if your Q4 attribution model still leans on platform-reported ROAS.

JOB MOVES: A former VP Marketing at a national furniture retailer has joined a Series B kitchenware startup as CMO. A well-known agency creative director is leaving to launch an independent studio.

PLATFORM WATCH: One major social platform quietly rolled back a controversial change to how it weights recency versus engagement in its main feed algorithm after publishers reported a sharp drop in referral traffic over the last two weeks — the kind of change that rarely gets an official announcement but shows up immediately in analytics dashboards. If your organic reach dipped unexpectedly in late June, this may be why, and it may also explain why it's since partially recovered.

CREATOR ECONOMY: A new report on creator partnership rates shows a widening gap between micro-influencers (10K-100K followers) and mid-tier creators (100K-500K), with brands increasingly favoring the former for cost efficiency despite lower individual reach — the logic being that a coordinated slate of ten micro-creators now often outperforms a single mid-tier partnership on both cost-per-engagement and perceived authenticity, according to the brands surveyed.

AGENCY WATCH, CONTINUED: Several holding companies are reportedly in early talks about further consolidation among their performance marketing units, following a similar deal announced last quarter. Independent shops we spoke with are split on whether this creates opportunity (clients fleeing bureaucracy) or existential risk (pricing pressure from bigger competitors).

That's it for today — see you tomorrow.

body_text:
Hey Jordan,

Attaching the first full round of creative for Gather, the holiday campaign. This is the concept we walked through at kickoff, now fleshed out across hero, email, and paid social formats.

Quick rundown of what's in the deck:

1. Hero concept - warm, low-lit tablescape photography, three color stories (Cranberry, Sage, Oat) that map to our three gifting collections. This replaces the bright studio-white look we used for spring/summer.
2. Typography - we're proposing a new display serif (Canela) for headlines only, keeping body copy in the existing Inter family so it doesn't feel like a full rebrand, just a seasonal shift.
3. Email templates - three variants ready: gift guide, countdown/urgency, and the post-Cyber-Monday "still shopping" nudge. Ben's lifecycle team already has the countdown one in Klaviyo as a draft.
4. Paid social - 9x16 and 1x1 crops for both the hero tablescape shot and three product-only cutdowns, plus a UGC-style set shot on a phone for TikTok that intentionally looks less polished.
5. OOH concept (stretch, budget-dependent) - a single static board concept for the Domain and South Congress locations if Wes can find room after the agency renewal numbers settle.

Things I need from you specifically before this goes to Sofia for final sign-off:
- Confirm the Cranberry palette doesn't clash with the new sitewide banner color once the replatform ships (I don't have visibility into what Anchor & Vine locked in).
- A gut check on whether the Canela headline treatment reads too editorial for our customer - it's a departure and I want your read before I fall in love with it.
- Sign-off on using the phone-shot UGC set for TikTok even though it wasn't part of the Northlight shoot brief; we'd need Hollis to add a half day for it.

I know Q4 is a lot right now with the agency contract and the site migration both live. Happy to walk through this live tomorrow if that's faster than comments in the deck. Target is to lock hero direction by the 18th so production has runway.

One more thing while I have you: I want to loop the popup and cart-abandonment flows into this too, since right now they're still running the spring photography and it'll look jarring once the homepage flips over to Gather. Ben's team can swap the creative in Klaviyo quickly once we have final assets, but I'd rather we plan for it now than scramble in October. Same question applies to the order-confirmation email template, which nobody ever thinks about updating seasonally but customers do see it right after checkout.

On budget and timeline: production cost for this round, assuming the TikTok add, comes in around $6,800 for stock, styling props, and Northlight's day rate beyond what's already covered in the retainer. Wes has a placeholder for it in the Q4 creative line but I wanted you to have the real number before it surprises him. Full asset delivery timeline, if we lock direction by the 18th, is first selects by August 20th and a complete set - email, paid social, and site imagery - by September 5th, which still gives the replatform team time to drop the new imagery into staging before their freeze.

Rachel

body_text:
Team,

We need to land the final creative concept for the holiday campaign this week so Fold & Field has enough runway to produce everything before BFCM. I've been sitting with the three directions from last week's review and want to lay out where my head is, but I want real pushback if you disagree — this decision is expensive to unwind once production starts.

DIRECTION A — 'Gathered' (the minimalist, editorial one): clean product shots on neutral backgrounds, heavy whitespace, very restrained typography. Pros: cheapest to produce, fastest turnaround, on-brand with our spring campaign so there's visual continuity. Cons: doesn't feel very 'holiday,' risk of blending into the crowded promo inbox in November.

DIRECTION B — 'Warm Nights' (the lifestyle one): full sets built out as cozy living rooms and dining scenes, warm lighting, models, the whole thing. This is the one that tested best in the June concept survey — respondents specifically called out feeling 'want to be in that room.' Pros: strongest emotional pull, most differentiated from competitors who are all doing clean minimalist holiday campaigns this year. Cons: expensive — full set builds, casting, multi-day shoot — and the most schedule risk given how tight our September production window already is.

DIRECTION C — 'Gift Guide First' (the utility one): leads with gifting categories and price points rather than mood, closer to what Denise's ecommerce team wants for conversion. Pros: cheapest, fastest, plays well with paid social direct-response ads. Cons: least brand-building, feels more like a retailer than Habitat Goods.

Budget envelope for creative production is roughly $85K regardless of which direction we pick — that number doesn't flex much either way.

One more thing worth naming: last year we made this exact call in late September, which left almost no cushion when the set builder ran two weeks over on the winter cabin concept. I don't want to repeat that. If we're doing B, I need everyone's honest read on schedule risk now, not a polite 'sure, sounds doable' that turns into a September fire drill. If the honest answer is that B is too tight given everything else on the calendar (the replatform QA window, the Amara whitelisting campaign, PR's Business Insider push), I'd rather hear that today and fall back to A or C than find out in three weeks.

I want to make the call by end of week. Please reply with your honest take by Friday — Rachel, especially want your read on production feasibility for B given the timeline; Cam, how each direction supports the content calendar; Tessa, ballpark cost delta between B and the other two if you have it offhand.

Thanks all,
Sofia

- The $120K is the Q4 paid social number, down from the $150K I floated back in June planning. I pulled it back after Nina's attribution pass showed we were over-crediting Meta prospecting for conversions email/SMS was actually driving.

snippet: Jordan, Here's where things stand post the FTC's updated endorsement guidance. Three things to build into the contract and the creative brief: 1. Disclosure placement - #ad or #spo
body_text:
Jordan,

Here's where things stand post the FTC's updated endorsement guidance. Three things to build into the contract and the creative brief:

1. Disclosure placement - #ad or #sponsored has to be unavoidable, meaning it can't be buried in a string of hashtags at the bottom of a caption. For Reels specifically, the FTC wants it in the video itself (on-screen text or verbal) as well as the caption, not caption-only anymore. Give Amara's team the exact language: "Paid partnership with Habitat Goods" using Instagram's built-in Paid Partnership tag, plus a spoken or on-screen "#ad" in the first three seconds.

2. Giveaway mechanics - if the mechanic is "tag a friend to enter," we need official rules posted somewhere (a linked page is fine), no purchase necessary language, odds of winning, entry period start/end dates, and eligibility (18+, US residents, employees of Habitat Goods and immediate family excluded). I'd also recommend capping it at one entry per person to avoid it reading as a sweepstakes requiring a bond in Texas - if you want, I can draft the official rules page copy, just tell me the entry window.

3. Material connection disclosure survives even if we don't pay her directly in cash - since she's getting product plus a fee, that's a material connection regardless of amount, so the disclosure requirement applies in full either way.

Send me the final contract once it's drafted and I'll do a quick pass before it goes to her for signature. Should be a fast turnaround on my end.

subject: Marketing Brew: the loyalty program arms race
snippet: Together with a sponsor you'll skim past — let's get into it. THE BIG STORY: Loyalty programs are having a moment again, and not the punch-card kind. Paid loyalty tiers — think $99
body_text:
Together with a sponsor you'll skim past — let's get into it.

THE BIG STORY: Loyalty programs are having a moment again, and not the punch-card kind. Paid loyalty tiers — think $99/year for free shipping, early access, and members-only drops — are spreading well beyond the retailers that made them famous. We talked to marketing leads at six DTC brands who've launched or are building a paid tier this year. The pitch to leadership is consistent: paid members spend 2-4x more annually than free members and churn less, but the upfront lift is real — most brands underestimate the customer service load a paid tier creates once members expect white-glove treatment.

One home goods operator (unnamed, mid-eight-figure revenue) told us their biggest surprise wasn't the tech build, it was pricing psychology: testing showed $79/year converted better than both $49 and $99, landing in a sweet spot that felt 'serious but not scary.'

WHY IT MATTERS: With acquisition costs still climbing across paid social, loyalty is one of the few levers marketing teams fully control without fighting a platform algorithm. But several brand leaders warned against copying the model wholesale — a paid tier only works if there's a genuinely differentiated benefit behind it, not just a 10% discount with a subscription fee attached.

ALSO IN THE INBOX:
- A major social platform is testing a new ad format that blends shoppable video with live chat — early advertiser feedback is mixed on measurement.
- Email deliverability rules are tightening again; if your bounce rate crept up after the last major inbox provider update, you're not alone.
- A roundup of the best-performing UGC ad formats this quarter, by category.

STAT OF THE DAY: 34% — the average share of paid budget consumer brands now allocate to paid social, per new survey data, with retail media eating into what used to be display and programmatic spend.

READER MAILBAG: Last week we asked how brands are handling the shift to first-party data collection. A lifecycle lead at a home goods company (name withheld) wrote in to say their quiz-based email capture flow — a short 'find your style' quiz that gates a discount code behind three questions — now outperforms their old static popup by 3x on conversion, with the added benefit of usable zero-party data for segmentation. A few other readers pushed back, arguing quizzes add friction that isn't worth it below a certain traffic threshold. We'll keep tracking the debate.

ONE MORE STAT: Brands that segment their loyalty communications by tenure (new member vs. year-two-plus) reported 22% higher engagement on those emails than brands sending the same content to all loyalty members regardless of how long they've been enrolled — a reminder that 'loyalty' isn't a single audience.

One more thing: we're hiring a retail reporter — know someone good? Reply and tell us.

body_text:
Hi Jordan,

One or more ads in your account "Habitat Goods — Search & Shopping" (412-908-6631) were disapproved for violating our Misleading Representation policy. This affects the "Fall Sale — Up to 50% Off" search campaign, which has been paused for the affected ad group.

WHAT WAS FLAGGED
Ad group: Fall Sale - Broad Match
Headline flagged: "Everything 50% Off — Today Only"
Reason: Our systems found this claim to be misleading because the sitewide discount referenced does not apply to your full catalog, and "today only" language was used across a promotion that has run for 11 consecutive days. This falls under our policy on exaggerated claims and false urgency, which prohibits advertising that creates a false sense of scarcity or time pressure that doesn't reflect the actual offer.

WHAT THIS MEANS
- The disapproved ads will not serve until the issue is resolved.
- Other ads in the same campaign are unaffected and continue to serve normally.
- Repeated policy violations across your account can lead to ad group, campaign, or account-level suspension.

HOW TO FIX IT
1. Edit the disapproved headline to accurately reflect the offer (e.g. reference the actual discount range, such as "Up to 50% Off Select Styles," and remove "today only" if the promotion is ongoing).
2. Resubmit the ad for review. Most reviews complete within 1 business day, though some can take longer.
3. If you believe this was flagged in error, you can request a manual review from the Policy Manager section of your account.

We also flagged two additional headlines in the same ad group as borderline and recommend reviewing your full Fall Sale headline set before resubmitting, to avoid a second review cycle. The borderline headlines were "Last Chance — Ends Tonight" and "Prices This Low Won't Last," both of which use similar urgency framing and are likely to draw the same scrutiny once a human reviewer looks at the ad group following the first disapproval.

WHY THIS MATTERS
Your account currently has a "Good" policy standing, but two disapprovals within a 90-day window can trigger a policy standing downgrade, which can slow down approval times for future campaigns, including your planned Q4 holiday launch. A downgraded account also loses access to some beta features and can see slower turnaround on manual review requests, which matters if you're planning to launch time-sensitive holiday creative in November.

WHAT WE RECOMMEND BEFORE YOU RESUBMIT
- Replace absolute claims ("Everything," "Today Only") with qualified language that matches the actual promotion mechanics in your checkout.
- Make sure any percentage-off claim matches the actual discount code logic — our reviewers now spot-check landing pages against ad copy.
- If the promotion is meant to run for multiple days, avoid "today only," "ends tonight," or countdown-style language unless there's a real countdown timer tied to an actual end date.
- Consider a policy pre-check pass on all Q4 holiday ad copy before launch, given the volume you're planning to run in November and December.

If you have questions, you can reach our policy support team through the Help Center or by replying to this notification with your account ID. Most manual review requests are resolved within 2 business days, but during Q4 ramp-up volume can push that closer to 4-5 business days, so we'd recommend getting ahead of any holiday creative review well before your planned launch dates.

body_text:
Jordan,

Flagging something before you see it elsewhere - Modern Retail published a piece this morning in their "Sourcing" newsletter titled "The gap between what DTC home brands say and what they ship," and Habitat Goods is named, not as the main subject but in a section about sustainability claims. The specific line: a former employee (unnamed, described only as "a former merchandising staffer") is quoted saying the "responsibly sourced" language on our linen and wood product pages overstates what's actually verified, and that internally the standard was "vendor self-attestation, not third-party certification."

CONTEXT: This isn't a fabrication, exactly - our sourcing claims page does rely on supplier questionnaires rather than something like GOTS or FSC certification for most SKUs, which has always been true and is disclosed (thinly) in a footnote. The unflattering framing is new, the underlying fact pattern mostly isn't.

SCALE: This is not a viral moment. The newsletter has a trade audience of maybe 40,000 subscribers, mostly retail/DTC operators and journalists, not consumers. I've seen it shared by two industry accounts on LinkedIn so far with neutral, not-outraged captions. No consumer press has picked it up as of 9am.

1. A short internal talking point for Sofia and the exec team in case anyone gets asked about it directly (by press, by a retail partner, at a conference).
2. A look at whether we want to quietly firm up the sourcing claims language on the site - not as a reaction to this piece, but because the underlying gap is real and someone else could raise it again with more reach.
3. I'd hold off reaching out to the reporter. Engaging tends to extend the life of a story that would otherwise die in 48 hours.

Want to sync at 2pm today? I can have the talking points draft ready by then.

For what it's worth, this is a fairly normal pattern for a company our size once you're doing enough volume to attract trade press attention - I've handled three or four of these for other DTC clients this year alone, usually tied to sourcing, labor, or return-policy claims, and the ones that turn into real problems are almost always the ones where the brand goes on the defensive publicly rather than just quietly tightening the underlying practice. I don't think this is that, but wanted to give you the pattern-matching context rather than just the recommendation.

Priyanka

body_text:
Team — pulled together a real retro on July before we lock the Q4 plan, because I don't want to repeat mistakes just because we're moving fast. This is longer than usual, worth the read.

WHAT WORKED
- The mid-July flash sale outperformed plan by 22% — Ben's segmented send (excluding anyone who'd bought in the last 14 days) clearly mattered, open rates were up almost 6 points over our usual blanket sends. We should make this the default approach going forward, not a one-off.
- TikTok organic (Cam's founder-story series) drove more qualified traffic than any paid channel per dollar spent, which is zero dollars. We're underinvesting in this relative to the return.
- The Amplitude cohort work Nina did on attribution finally gave us a real answer on the branded search question instead of arguing about it in meetings for the fourth quarter in a row.

WHAT DIDN'T
- Paid social CPMs on Meta were up 34% month over month and we didn't catch it until the monthly close, by which point we'd already overspent the channel by about $4,200. Wes flagged this and he's right that we need weekly pacing checks, not monthly.
- The homepage A/B test Rachel and Nina ran got contaminated partway through — a cache issue meant some users saw both variants across sessions. We don't have clean results and need to rerun it in August with better QA on the test setup itself.
- I sat on the paid social budget question too long before looping Sofia in properly, which meant she went into the July leadership review less prepared than she should have been. That's on me, and it's part of why I over-communicated on the budget memo this week — trying not to repeat it.

WHAT CHANGES FOR Q4
1. Weekly, not monthly, spend pacing reviews starting in August. Wes is going to send a Friday actuals-vs-plan number to me and Sofia.
2. More investment in organic social content given the TikTok results — Cam, let's talk about whether we need help scaling the founder-story format.
3. Any test that touches the homepage gets a dry-run QA pass before it goes live, no exceptions, even under deadline pressure.
4. I'm going to loop Sofia in earlier and more often on anything budget-related, even before it's fully baked, rather than waiting until I have a polished answer.

Good quarter overall, genuinely. Want us to end Q4 the same way.

Jordan

subject: Re: Q3 Channel Attribution — Numbers Don't Match
snippet: On Mon, Jul 27, 2026 at 9:30 AM Wes Duffy <wes.duffy@habitatgoods.com> wrote: > Jordan — running into a discrepancy building the Q3 board slide on channel performance. Finance's mo
body_text:
On Mon, Jul 27, 2026 at 9:30 AM Wes Duffy <wes.duffy@habitatgoods.com> wrote:
> Jordan — running into a discrepancy building the Q3 board slide on channel performance. Finance's model, using last-touch attribution off the Shopify order data, has paid channels driving 31% of Q3 revenue. The marketing dashboard Nina's team maintains shows 48% using whatever multi-touch model is behind it. That's a big enough gap that I don't want to just pick one and hope nobody asks. Which number should go in the board deck, due Aug 14?

Happy to walk through why these differ, since it's a real methodology gap and not a data error on either side.

Finance's last-touch model only credits the very last click before checkout. So if a customer sees a paid social ad, doesn't click, comes back three days later through an organic search for 'Habitat Goods sectional,' and converts — that entire order gets attributed to organic search, and paid social gets zero credit, even though it's very plausibly what put the brand in front of them in the first place.

Our model is position-based: 40% credit to the first touch, 40% to the last touch, and the remaining 20% split evenly across any touches in between. Using a real example from last week — a customer's journey was: saw a Meta ad on July 19 (no click), clicked a TikTok ad on July 21, opened a retargeting email on July 23, then converted via a direct site visit on July 24 after searching the brand name. Last-touch gives 100% of that order to 'direct/organic branded search,' which tells you almost nothing useful, since the customer wouldn't have searched the brand name at all without the two paid touches earlier in the week. Our model splits that order 40% Meta, 40% TikTok, 20% email, which I'd argue is a much more honest picture of what actually drove the sale.

Neither number is 'wrong' exactly — they're answering different questions. Last-touch tells you what closed the sale. Multi-touch tells you what built the pipeline that led to the sale. The problem is using only one of them to make budget decisions, because last-touch systematically undercounts upper-funnel paid spend and multi-touch can overcount if you're not careful about the weighting.

For what it's worth, I'd push back on us reporting last-touch alone to the board — 31% badly understates what paid is actually doing for us, and if that number gets used to justify a Q4 paid budget cut, we'd be making a real strategic mistake off of an incomplete picture.

meta.action_summary: Review the multi-touch attribution methodology before it's used in the board deck.

snippet: Sofia — wanted to walk you through the paid search decision before it shows up in the Q4 plan, since I know you'll ask and I'd rather you hear the reasoning from me than infer it f
body_text:
Sofia — wanted to walk you through the paid search decision before it shows up in the Q4 plan, since I know you'll ask and I'd rather you hear the reasoning from me than infer it from a spreadsheet:

- We're cutting branded search spend by about 60% starting October. Branded terms were basically capturing demand we'd already generated through email and paid social — Nina ran a geo-holdout test in June and branded search conversions barely moved when we paused it in three test markets.
- Non-branded search stays roughly flat, that's still finding new customers, just at a much higher CAC than social right now ($54 vs $31 blended).
- The dollars we're freeing up (~$18K/month) are going into the paid social number I sent you last week, not into a new channel — I didn't want to spread us thinner across five channels when we're already stretched on creative production.
- Risk I want to flag honestly: if a competitor starts bidding aggressively on our brand terms while we're not defending them, we could see some erosion. I'm comfortable with that risk through Q4 based on the holdout data, but I want you to know it's a real trade-off, not a free lunch.
- Google rep is aware and not thrilled, for what it's worth, but that's expected.

Happy to walk through the holdout test methodology if you want to poke holes in it before this goes to the board deck.

Jordan
body_html:
Sofia — wanted to walk you through the paid search decision before it shows up in the Q4 plan.

snippet: Jordan, As we head into the last full planning push before Q4, wanted to put in writing where I think our priorities need to sit so we're aligned before you build out the departmen
body_text:
Jordan,

As we head into the last full planning push before Q4, wanted to put in writing where I think our priorities need to sit so we're aligned before you build out the department OKRs.

1. HOLIDAY CAMPAIGN — this is the single biggest lever we have this quarter. Between the creative direction (still being finalized, I know) and the media plan, I want this locked with zero ambiguity by the first week of September. BFCM is non-negotiable — we cannot repeat last year's late-approval scramble where the agency was still turning around assets 4 days before launch.

2. RETENTION / LIFECYCLE — Ben's abandoned cart and post-purchase flow work has been quietly good this year, and I think there's real headroom left. I'd like a proposal from you on whether we invest further here in Q4 or hold steady and focus resources on acquisition given the holiday push. Genuinely open on this one, want your read.

3. WEBSITE REPLATFORM — launch date has already moved once (now Aug 17 per Nina), and the timing is uncomfortably close to when we need go-to-market assets locked for holiday. Want a contingency plan in case it slips again — what does the campaign look like if we're still running on the old site template through the holiday launch?

4. AGENCY RELATIONSHIP — the Fold & Field retainer renewal needs to close out before Q1, and given how much production load is shifting onto them for the holiday campaign, I want to make sure the new scope actually reflects what we're asking them to do, not just a rubber-stamp of last year's terms.

5. BUDGET DISCIPLINE — finance has been clear that overall marketing spend needs to flex with margin pressure this quarter (you saw Wes's note on paid social). I'd rather we get ahead of this proactively department-wide than have individual budget lines get cut reactively in November.

None of this is meant to be exhaustive — I know you've got your own read on priorities too, and I want this to be a conversation, not a directive. Let's grab 45 minutes this week to talk through it before you finalize the OKR doc. I'd like to review a draft before it goes to the broader team, ideally by August 21st so we have runway to socialize it before the offsite.

Thanks for everything you're carrying right now — I know Q4 planning season is a lot on top of the day-to-day.

subject: Content Calendar — Q4 Editorial Strategy
snippet: Jordan, Wanted to get you the full Q4 editorial strategy before our sync Friday so you have time to react. Here's where my head's at. BLOG: Shifting from our current 2x/week genera
body_text:
Jordan,

Wanted to get you the full Q4 editorial strategy before our sync Friday so you have time to react. Here's where my head's at.

BLOG: Shifting from our current 2x/week general lifestyle cadence to a themed-month structure — September is 'Small Space Solutions' (ties to the back-to-school apartment-furnishing traffic we see every year), October is 'Hosting Season' (leads naturally into the holiday gifting push), November-December is full gift-guide mode with weekly refreshes based on inventory and what's trending in paid social. This gives us a clearer narrative thread than the somewhat scattered approach we've had, and lets SEO content compound instead of competing with itself across too many topics at once.

EMAIL/SMS EDITORIAL SUPPORT: Coordinating closely with Ben on lifecycle so editorial content (styling guides, care tips, behind-the-scenes sourcing stories) feeds directly into flows rather than living only on the blog. The reclaimed-wood sourcing story specifically tested really well as email content in the spring — I want three more pieces in that same 'origin story' format for Q4, likely tied to the holiday campaign's Direction B lifestyle sets — or Direction C now, I saw the thread.

SOCIAL: Leaning further into UGC given how well the TikTok creative refresh performed in Q3 (Nina's recap has the numbers — CAC and ROAS both meaningfully better than our produced content). Want to formalize a small UGC budget line separate from the paid whitelisting spend so we're not treating it as an afterthought.

PR TIE-INS: Priyanka's team has three placements in the pipeline for Q4 (Business Insider ran, two more pending) and I want blog/social content ready to amplify each one within 24 hours of publication rather than the usual week-later scramble.

HEADCOUNT: Flagging early — if we add the UGC program and the origin-story email series on top of the existing blog cadence, I think I need either a part-time contractor or a shift in my own priorities. Not asking for a decision now, just want it on your radar before Q4 actually starts.

MEASUREMENT: One thing I want to fix from last quarter — we never agreed on what 'working' means for the blog beyond raw sessions. Proposing we track assisted conversions from blog-sourced sessions specifically, plus email signups attributed to content, so we're not just reporting traffic that doesn't tie back to anything Sofia or finance cares about. I can pull last year's numbers as a baseline if that's useful before Friday.

TIMELINE RISK: The themed-month structure only works if September content is locked by August 22nd at the latest — anything later and we lose the back-to-school traffic window entirely, since that search demand falls off a cliff after Labor Day. I'd rather flag that constraint now than discover it the week we're supposed to publish.

Let me know if any of this conflicts with where you and Sofia are landing on overall priorities — happy to adjust before Friday.

Cam

snippet: On Wed, Aug 5, 2026 at 10:00 AM Nina Sokolov <nina.sokolov@habitatgoods.com> wrote: > Can make the test work. For a clean read by Oct 20 (so we have time to roll out the winner bef
body_text:
On Wed, Aug 5, 2026 at 10:00 AM Nina Sokolov <nina.sokolov@habitatgoods.com> wrote:
> Can make the test work. For a clean read by Oct 20 (so we have time to roll out the winner before Nov 1) we need roughly 40K sessions per arm, which we'll clear in about 6 days at current holiday-adjacent traffic. Only catch: if the shoot direction changes because of the test, that eats into the buffer we have for finishing paid social creative. So whichever way this goes, we need final photography locked by Oct 12 at the latest.

Okay, spent yesterday building both directions properly instead of just mocking swatches, so here's a fuller writeup before we ship this to test.

Variant A (moody): pulls from the Q3 lifestyle shoot — warm, low three-quarter light, product staged in a lived-in room setting, muted sage and terracotta palette. Copy sits in a semi-transparent dark scrim so it stays legible against the darker background. This is the direction I think best represents where the brand is headed for FY27 — every competitor in the DTC home space right now is doing bright, punchy, primary-color hero banners and I think we stand out more by not doing that.

Variant B (bright): uses the Q3 PDP product photography Denise referenced — white background, high key lighting, saturated accent colors on the CTA. Copy sits on a solid color block instead of over the image, which is part of why it tests well: less visual noise competing for attention, cleaner scan path to the button.

Both variants keep the same copy hierarchy Cam wrote (headline, subhead, single CTA) so the test isolates image/palette rather than confounding it with copy changes. I also cut the confetti graphic from both per Sofia's note, and swapped 'Cozy Season Starts Here' for 'The Season, Reimagined' as the backup line since legal flagged the original — can revisit if we want something punchier once we're not worried about IP.

One more constraint worth flagging: if Variant A wins, we can ship with existing assets. If Variant B wins outright, we're mostly fine too since it's built on Q3 photography we already have licensed. Where it gets expensive is if the test comes back close and someone wants a hybrid — that would need net-new photography and we're tight on the calendar for that.

Links to both are updated in the same Figma file. Would love signoff from everyone by end of day Monday (Aug 10) so we can hand off to Nina's team with buffer before the Oct 12 photography lock she mentioned.

Rachel Lindqvist
Brand Design Lead, Habitat Goods

snippet: Hi Jordan, Here's your Weekly Anomaly Digest for Habitat Goods (Aug 3 - Aug 9). Three metrics were flagged by our detection models this week. 1. EMAIL-ATTRIBUTED REVENUE — UP 34% E
body_text:
Hi Jordan,

Here's your Weekly Anomaly Digest for Habitat Goods (Aug 3 - Aug 9). Three metrics were flagged by our detection models this week.

1. EMAIL-ATTRIBUTED REVENUE — UP 34%
Email-attributed revenue rose from a weekly average of $61,200 to $82,100, a 34% increase. This tracks with the "Back to School Flash Sale" campaign that went out 7/18 and the follow-up cart abandonment flow Ben set up in June — attribution modeling shows roughly 60% of the lift coming from returning customers who opened but didn't click on the first send, then converted off the second-touch reminder. No action needed here, flagging as a positive anomaly worth noting for the Q4 planning offsite deck.

2. NEW USER SIGNUP RATE — DOWN 12%
New account creation on the site is down 12% week over week, concentrated in organic search traffic (-19%) rather than paid (-3%) or direct (-1%). This lines up with a broader dip in organic sessions that started the week of 7/27, which may be related to a Google core update — worth checking Search Console for ranking movement on your top 20 landing pages. Paid and lifecycle channels are compensating for most of the volume, so total revenue is not currently at risk, but the trend is worth watching for another week before treating it as noise.

3. SESSION DURATION ON PDP (PRODUCT DETAIL PAGE) — DOWN 9%
Average session duration on product detail pages dropped 9%, most visible on the new "Linen Collection" pages that launched 8/1. This could indicate the new page layout is either working very well (fast add-to-cart, less browsing needed) or underperforming (users bouncing quickly). Add-to-cart rate on these pages is flat, and bounce rate is up 4 points, which leans toward the latter explanation. Recommend a quick session-replay review before drawing conclusions.

WHAT WE'D FLAG FOR THE OFFSITE DECK
The email revenue lift (#1) is a good data point for the lifecycle section of the Q4 plan. The organic dip (#2) is worth a line in the risks section even if it resolves on its own — better to have flagged it than not. The PDP session duration change (#3) probably doesn't need its own slide, but worth a footnote if anyone asks why bounce rate ticked up on the new template.

A NOTE ON METHODOLOGY
These anomalies are flagged relative to a rolling 8-week baseline that automatically excludes known promotional spikes (like the Back to School Flash Sale) so seasonal noise doesn't drown out real signal. If a metric you'd expect to see here — like paid social CAC or the lifecycle flow performance Ben has been tuning — isn't included, it's most likely because it's still within one standard deviation of its baseline and didn't clear our flagging threshold this week. You can adjust sensitivity per-metric from the Anomaly Detection settings panel if you'd like tighter or looser thresholds heading into the higher-volume Q4 stretch.

As always, you can dig into any of these in the live dashboard, and this digest will auto-adjust its baselines as more data comes in. If the organic dip hasn't resolved by next week's digest, we'll escalate it from a soft flag to a tracked anomaly with its own trend line.

— The Amplitude Team
